nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the comic thriller and the Berry books
literary_identity: Novelist; the pseudonym of Cecil William Mercer, the author of the Berry books and one of the most popular comic thriller writers of the century.
biography: Born Cecil William Mercer at Walmer, Kent, on 7 August 1885; he practised law and wrote the Berry books — The Brother of Daphne (1914), The Courts of the Morning (1929), Jonah and Co. (1922) — and the Chandos thrillers, publishing some thirty novels. He died in exile in Rhodesia on 5 March 1960.
literary_profile: Dornford Yates wrote the funniest comic thrillers of the century: his Berry books and his Chandos novels created the gentleman-adventurer comedy in which the dialogue and the farce are as important as the plot, and they made him one of the most popular writers of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The comic dialogue of the gentleman-adventurer; the absurd plot of pursuit and disguise; the English country house and the Continental hotel; the upper-class slang; the plain, elegant, funny prose.
intellectual_concerns: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; the absurd, the void.
historical_significance: Dornford Yates wrote the funniest comic thrillers of the century: his Berry books and his Chandos novels created the gentleman-adventurer comedy, and they made him one of the most popular writers of the period.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the thriller and the mass-market crime novel
literary_identity: Journalist, novelist and screenwriter; the most prolific and most widely read crime writer of the century.
biography: Born Richard Horatio Edgar Wallace in Greenwich on 1 April 1875; he served in the army and as a war correspondent, and published The Four Just Men in 1905, followed by some 170 novels, including the Sanders of the River stories, The Ringer (1925) and The Door with Seven Locks (1926). He died in Hollywood on 10 February 1932.
literary_profile: Edgar Wallace was the most prolific and most widely read crime writer of the century: his some 170 novels created the modern thriller, the mass-market crime novel and the screen story, and his Four Just Men and The Ringer made him the founder of the British thriller industry.
stylistic_characteristics: The rapid plot of pursuit and revelation; the grotesque villain and the comic detective; the colonial setting and the London underworld; the plain, breathless, serial prose; the twist in the last chapter.
intellectual_concerns: The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital; empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent; money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination.
historical_significance: Edgar Wallace was the most prolific and most widely read crime writer of the century: his some 170 novels created the modern thriller, the mass-market crime novel and the screen story, and his work made him the founder of the British thriller industry.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Georgian war lyric of Into Battle
literary_identity: Poet and soldier; the officer-poet of 'Into Battle', the most argued-over lyric of the first year of the war.
biography: Born Julian Henry Francis Grenfell in London on 30 March 1888, the son of Lord Desborough; he was educated at Eton and Balliol College, Oxford, and commissioned into the Royal Dragoons in 1910. He served in France from October 1914, was wounded in May 1915, and died of his wounds on 26 May 1915, days after 'Into Battle' appeared in The Times and in the second edition of his Poems. His letters and journals were published posthumously.
literary_profile: Julian Grenfell stands at the centre of the argument about the poetry of 1914-15: 'Into Battle', with its exultant acceptance of death in the open air, was taken by his generation's critics as the type of the lyric that the later war poetry had to answer, and it remains the test case in every account of how the Georgian lyric met the trench. His letters and journals, equally vivid, are the prose companion to the poem.
stylistic_characteristics: The long, swelling, sunlit line of the Georgian lyric; the exultant apostrophe to death and to the body in the open; the exact observation of the French landscape from the saddle; the rhyme that carries the line rather than closes it; the prose of the letters, equally visual and equally unguarded.
intellectual_concerns: The body in the open air and the joy of physical life; the English and French countryside as the ground of the lyric; war as fulfilment rather than sacrifice; the officer's eye for the landscape and the horse; the elegy that refuses to be elegiac.
historical_significance: Julian Grenfell's 'Into Battle' is the most famous and most contested lyric of the war's first year: read by his contemporaries as the voice of the happy soldier and by the later war poets as the voice that had to be answered, it fixed the terms of the argument about 1914 and remains the type of the Georgian lyric turned to war.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the sailing adventure of the Lake District and the Swallows series
literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the creator of Swallows and Amazons and of the great sailing novels of English childhood.
biography: Born Arthur Michell Ransome at Leeds on 18 January 1884, the son of a history professor; he read chemistry at Yorkshire College and went to London to write, publishing Bohemia in London (1907) and A History of Storytelling (1909), and serving as a foreign correspondent in Russia, where he witnessed the revolution and married Trotsky's secretary, Evgenia Shveliepina. From 1930 the sailing novels made him the most read writer of English childhood; he died at Manchester on 3 June 1967.
literary_profile: Arthur Ransome invented the sailing novel of English childhood: the Swallows and Amazons series took the practical detail of boats, camps, charts and weather and made it the whole substance of adventure, so that the children's own competence is the plot. His Russia books and his journalism are forgotten beside them, but the series remains the standard against which every English children's adventure of the open air is measured.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, exact, practical prose of the sailor; the chart, the knot, the meal and the weather reported as the adventure itself; the dialogue of children left competently alone; the absence of adults except as distant authorities; the Lake District and the Norfolk Broads rendered with a navigator's exactness.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood competence and the children's own republic; the boat, the camp and the chart as the instruments of imagination; the English lake and broad as the theatre of adventure; the Russian revolution witnessed at first hand; the quarrel between the journalist's eye and the novelist's loyalty.
historical_significance: Arthur Ransome's Swallows and Amazons series is the founding cycle of the English sailing novel for children: its practical exactness, its children's republic and its Lake District water made competence the substance of adventure and gave English childhood its classic open-air fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the inventor of the modern high fantasy and the philologist of Beowulf
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and philologist; the author of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings and the Merton Professor of English Language at Oxford.
biography: Born John Ronald Reuel Tolkien at Bloemfontein on 3 January 1892; he was brought up in the West Midlands after his father's death, read English at Exeter College, Oxford, and served as a signals officer on the Somme in 1916. He held the Leeds chair of English Language and then the Rawlinson and Bosworth chair of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford, and from 1945 the Merton professorship; The Hobbit appeared in 1937 and The Lord of the Rings in 1954-55. He died at Bournemouth on 2 September 1973.
literary_profile: J. R. R. Tolkien created the modern high fantasy and, with it, the most read fiction of the twentieth century: The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings gave the invented world its grammar, its languages and its history, while 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' and On Fairy-Stories rewrote the theory of the northern epic and of faerie. His philology is the root of the fiction, and the fiction is the proof of his claim that a language grows a mythology.
stylistic_characteristics: The invented proper noun and the sounded language behind it; the slow, layered, annalistic narrative that reports a history rather than a plot; the comic homeliness of the hobbit set against the high style of the elves; the elegiac north; the sentence built on the rhythms of the Old English prose he edited.
intellectual_concerns: Language and the mythology it generates; the north, the heroic and the elegiac; faerie and the recovery of the marvellous; the machine and the dominion of the will over creation; the Roman Catholic imagination under the invented world; the fellowship and the refusal of the ring.
historical_significance: J. R. R. Tolkien is the inventor of the modern high fantasy and the most read novelist of the twentieth century: The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings gave the invented world its languages and its history, and his essays on Beowulf and on fairy-stories remain the founding criticism of the mode he created.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Christian apologist, the space trilogy and the allegory of love
literary_identity: Critic, novelist and apologist; the author of The Allegory of Love, the space trilogy and The Screwtape Letters.
biography: Born Clive Staples Lewis at Belfast on 29 November 1898; he served in the war, was wounded in 1918, and took the triple first at Oxford that began his fellowship at Magdalen College. The Allegory of Love (1936) made him a scholar of the first rank; his conversion of 1929-31 issued in The Pilgrim's Regress, The Problem of Pain and The Screwtape Letters, and the space trilogy carried the argument into fiction. He held the Cambridge chair of Medieval and Renaissance English from 1954 and died at Oxford on 22 November 1963.
literary_profile: C. S. Lewis is the central Christian writer of the English twentieth century and one of its great scholars: The Allegory of Love founded the modern study of the medieval allegorical imagination, the space trilogy and The Screwtape Letters turned the argument about belief into fiction of the first order, and his broadcasts made the case for Christianity the common property of the reading public.
stylistic_characteristics: The lucid, conversational, argumentative prose that states the objection before the answer; the allegory built as a landscape to be crossed; the science fiction of the unfallen planet; the satire in the voice of the devil; the scholar's quotation worn lightly in the apologist's sentence.
intellectual_concerns: Allegory and the medieval imagination; belief and the argument from desire; the unfallen world and the fall of the will; the devil as bureaucrat; joy and the inconsolable longing; the quarrel with the scientific materialism of his own faculty.
historical_significance: C. S. Lewis is the central Christian writer of the English twentieth century: The Allegory of Love founded the modern study of medieval allegory, the space trilogy and The Screwtape Letters carried the argument about belief into fiction, and his apologetic prose remains the standard voice of the converted intellect.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Welsh; the tramp poet of Leisure and the Georgian lyric
literary_identity: Poet and autobiographer; the super-tramp of the Georgian anthologies and of 'Leisure'.
biography: Born William Henry Davies at Newport, Monmouthshire, on 3 July 1871; he lost a foot jumping a freight train in Ontario in 1899 and lived as a tramp and cattle-drover in Wales, England and North America until The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp (1908), with its introduction by George Bernard Shaw, made him a writer. The Georgian anthologies and 'Leisure' made him a household poet; he died at Nailsworth, Gloucestershire, on 26 September 1940.
literary_profile: W. H. Davies is the tramp poet of the Georgian lyric: The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp is the classic English account of the road, and 'Leisure' - 'What is this life if, full of care, we have no time to stand and stare' - is one of the most quoted short poems in the language. His plain, unadorned lyric of the roadside and the hedge gave the Georgian anthology its voice from below.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain short line and the plain word; the lyric of the roadside, the hedge and the open sky; the absence of the literary allusion and of the learned metaphor; the tramp's eye for weather, food and shelter; the quiet, unforced moral at the close of the lyric.
intellectual_concerns: The road and the life of the tramp; poverty, begging and the charity of the countryside; nature observed from the hedge rather than from the garden; the body's want and the sky's plenty; Wales and the Welsh border as the remembered home.
historical_significance: W. H. Davies is the tramp poet of the Georgian lyric: The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp is the classic English account of the road, and 'Leisure' is among the most quoted short poems in the language, the voice of the roadside in the anthology of the garden.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; Façade, the modernist lyric and the Sitwell little magazines
literary_identity: Poet and critic; the editor of Wheels and the author of Façade, the most performed experiment of English verse.
biography: Born Edith Louisa Sitwell at Scarborough on 7 September 1887, the eldest of the three poetic Sitwells; she edited the anthology Wheels against the Georgian anthologies and published The Mother and Other Poems (1915) and Clown's Houses (1916). Façade, the settings of her poems to William Walton's music, was first performed in 1923; Gold Coast Customs (1929) and Street Songs (1942), with 'Still Falls the Rain', mark her later, darker manner. She died in London on 9 December 1964.
literary_profile: Edith Sitwell is the central woman poet of English modernism before 1945: Façade made the sound of the poem its subject and remains the most performed experiment in English verse, the early lyrics gave the imagist and vorticist little magazines their most accomplished English contributor, and Street Songs carried the war elegy into the modernist idiom. Her criticism and her quarrels shaped the reception of the new poetry.
stylistic_characteristics: The poem as a pattern of sound: assonance, consonant-chime and the sprung line; the baroque image of the harlequin, the sun and the clown; the later deepening into the elegiac and the religious; the prose of the critic, combative and exact; the reading voice as part of the instrument.
intellectual_concerns: Sound and the autonomy of the poem; the mask, the clown and the harlequinade; the family and the wound of the childhood; the war elegy and the crucifixion; the quarrel with the Georgian anthologists and with the reviewers; aristocracy and the artist.
historical_significance: Edith Sitwell is the central woman poet of English modernism before 1945: Façade made the sound of the poem its subject, the early lyrics gave the little magazines their most accomplished English voice, and Street Songs carried the war elegy into the modernist idiom.
